opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about fundraising less as a goal and more as a tool. vLLM started as an open-source project, and what matters most to me is that it keeps being the inference engine people trust and build on. So when we think about capital, the first question is: what does the money let us do that we couldn't do otherwise?

Inference is becoming one of the biggest cost centers in AI. Every model that gets trained eventually has to be served, often billions of times. The engineering work to make that efficient across many kinds of hardware and model architectures is enormous, and you can't sustain it on goodwill alone. You need full-time engineers, serious compute for testing and benchmarking, and people who work closely with hardware vendors and model developers. That takes real resources.

At the same time, I'm careful about what kind of capital we take and from whom. An open-source project has a community, and that community has to believe the project won't be quietly turned into something closed. So we look for investors who understand that open source is the foundation of the strategy, not a marketing phase we'll grow out of. If someone's thesis is to lock things down later, we aren't a good fit, however good the terms are.

I also try to be honest about timing. There's a lot of excitement around AI, and it's tempting to raise as much as possible while the market is hot. But too much money too early can distort your priorities. You start optimizing for the story you told investors instead of what users actually need. I'd rather raise what lets us execute well on a clear plan and keep the team focused.

So the short answer: we raise capital to make vLLM sustainable and to push inference efficiency forward faster, and we try to do it in a way that protects the open-source community that made the project matter in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing investors who support open source, but does not attribute fundraising ease to relationships with investors who previously supported the project.

r002.rationale: It cautions against raising too much too early and favors raising enough to execute a clear plan, but does not state that further fundraising should be timed to the company’s growth.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about it very cautiously, because vLLM itself is not a company — it's an open-source project, and that distinction matters a lot to me. The project started at Berkeley, it grew because thousands of people contributed and trusted that it would stay neutral and open. Whatever we build commercially has to protect that trust, not spend it.

So when I talk to investors, the first thing I say is that the open-source project is not the product. We won't take features out of vLLM and put them behind a paywall, and we won't play the "open core" game where the community version slowly becomes a demo. The moment we do that, people will fork it, and they would be right to. The inference ecosystem moves too fast for anyone to hold a toll gate.

What a company can do is solve the problems that an open-source project structurally cannot. Enterprises want someone accountable: stable releases, long-term support, security patches, help integrating with their hardware and their internal serving stack. There is also the hardware side — every chip vendor wants vLLM to run well on their accelerators, and that's real engineering work that someone needs to fund. And then there's the operational layer above the engine: multi-node scheduling, disaggregated prefill and decode, cache management across a fleet. That's where a lot of the value sits, and it's much harder to just download.

On the actual raise, I'd rather take less money from people who understand open-source infrastructure than more from people expecting a consumer-style growth curve. Infrastructure businesses compound slowly at first. If you raise at a valuation that assumes you'll monetize the whole community, you create pressure to do exactly the things that destroy the community. I've watched that happen to other projects, and I don't want to repeat it.

The other thing I keep in mind is that most of the core maintainers are researchers and engineers, not salespeople. So I want the company to be a place where the best contributors can work on vLLM full-time and get paid well for it. If capital lets us do that — keep the project healthy, hire maintainers, and build a sustainable business on top without compromising the open part — then raising makes sense. If it doesn't, I'd rather stay small.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses choosing investors who understand open-source infrastructure, but does not attribute fundraising ease to relationships formed through earlier support for vLLM.

r002.rationale: The candidate says to raise cautiously and stay small if capital would compromise the project, but does not state that further fundraising should be timed to the company’s growth.

astra-6.text:
I think about raising capital as a way to support the work we want to do. With vLLM, that means asking: What does the community need, what do customers need, and where would a dedicated team help us move faster?

You need resources to hire people and to test and optimize across hardware. But I wouldn’t want fundraising itself to become the goal. The important thing is to build a sustainable business while keeping the open-source project useful and healthy. So I’d look for investors who understand that relationship and are willing to support it over the long term.

r001.rationale: The response says to seek investors who understand the open-source relationship, but does not attribute easier fundraising to relationships built through earlier support for the project.

r002.rationale: It discusses long-term support and sustainable growth, but does not say fundraising should be timed to the company’s growth.
